posts.content:
Our Treasury customers moved into two new mutual fund products, each over a single weekend, and it was so seamless almost nobody noticed. 

Fund migrations can take months and cause disruption along the way. For cash that businesses use to run payroll and pay vendors, that wasn't an option — so before Trevor J. Walters and the Investments team could launch the new offerings, they spent most of a year rebuilding what sits underneath them.

Reference data for every investment asset Treasury supports lived across 13 tables and 32 files. The team replaced it with a Security Master Service, creating a shared source of truth for market data, trading systems, and the Treasury ledger. Adding or changing an asset went from about a month of engineering work to one Ops instruction. "It's one of those critical pieces where nobody notices when it's working but everyone feels it when it's missing," Trevor said.

They also moved Mercury Treasury and Mercury Personal Invest onto Ascend, Apex's new real-time custodian infrastructure. Trading, account management and money movement now run on modern, real-time APIs instead of a legacy overnight batch system. This unlocked faster account opening and faster wire settlements into Treasury, so we can move as quickly as our customers do.
 
Then came the migrations themselves. Holdings moved from the old funds to the new ones over one weekend each, and customers logged in Monday to new, Mercury-exclusive funds that were already invested.

The unglamorous work is usually the real work. More on how this came together and what it unlocks for your business: https://lnkd.in/gmBm3Q7V

posts.content:
Brand Designers Sarah Mohammadi and Serena E. spent weeks on one texture. Not the color, not the shape. Just how it would feel against your thumb.

Mercury's IO card, designed by artist Simone Bodmer-Turner, shipped last week. A sculpture is a three dimensional object, layered, catching light from a dozen angles. A card is a flat rectangle that has to survive a wallet. Translating from sculpture to product is where the two designers spent most of their time.

Bodmer-Turner leaves her materials in whatever natural state they settle into, a patina, a rough edge, a surface that was never smoothed over. "It feels natural, as if it has always existed," Serena said. Getting that same quality onto something flat meant treating the card's surface itself as the material. "We wanted to go beyond adding an image of something special. We wanted to make people feel like they're holding a piece of art."

It started with how the sculpture was photographed. Sarah and the team studied every shadow and highlight in the reference shots, since a flat, evenly lit photo would have erased exactly the depth they were trying to preserve. Then came the detail almost nobody would guess took the longest: the crop, worked through what Sarah called "countless iterations to get the right balance of detail and abstraction."

posts.content:
Hannah had three budgets on one card and no idea which one dinner was about to hit.

She was at a Mercury onsite, testing the thing she'd spent months designing. Budgets is new in Mercury: rather than issuing an employee three cards for three purposes, a company sets money aside for each purpose — the lunch perk, the onsite, the office coffee run — and all of it lives on one card, each with its own limits and its own rules. Which is elegant right up until you're standing in a restaurant holding a bill that could plausibly belong to two of them, waiting to learn whether the system you built can tell the difference.

"The push notification came through and it had routed it to my lunch perk as expected, and also took care of categorization automatically, and automatically attached my receipt from my Gmail inbox because of our receipt matching feature," said Hannah Johnson, a product designer on Budgets. "I felt informed and relieved that everything had been automatically taken care of for me. Magical was definitely the feeling."

Most spend tools are built for the people in control — the finance leads, the admins, the controllers — while the employee experience gets sorted out afterward, which is how you end up with someone at a register trying to remember which card they're supposed to be using. Hannah's team started from the other end, on the premise that employees shouldn't have to think about the mechanics of company spending at all: they should know what they can spend on and how much, buy the thing, and trust that everything downstream gets handled.

So it gets handled. An auto-router reads the transaction and decides which budget it belongs to. Categorization happens on its own. Receipts match themselves out of your inbox, or arrive as a photo you text back. The only moment that asks anything of you is the one where your phone tells you it's already done.

“A principle across this work has been meeting employees where they are,” Hannah said. “These are people who are out running errands for the office, at onsites, at sales dinners, traveling. Given that, it felt important that our communication be really respectful and not overwhelming, but still reach them in the moments where it’s useful.”

At Mercury we are always trying to figure out what is standing between entrepreneurs and their next stage of growth, mirroring many policy conversations in D.C. about how to create the right policies to support the growth of American businesses.

We just launched the second year of our data report, and while it had many interesting findings on use of AI, impacts of AI on hiring, and business costs, one finding really stood out to me: 23% of founders had to turn away investment in the past 24 months, most often in the $100-500K range, and usually not by choice.  

Outdated crowdfunding audit thresholds, hitting the maximum investor count, and interested investor's fund restrictions were the most common reasons cited. It feels like a policy detail that's easy to gloss over, with so much else in the report, but represents a lot of capital that founders wanted and couldn't take. 

Results like these show that updating the rules that govern capital access for new and existing businesses is crucial to ensuring we have a healthy and growing economy that supports innovation.

posts.content:
"Craft" might be the most overused word in tech right now. It's in investor pitches, JDs, landing pages... it's used so much it's starting to feel meaningless.

Working on our limited edition card with sculptor Simone Bodmer-Turner reminded me what the word actually means. Two details from the project:
1. The first texture samples came back close, probably close enough that most teams would said good enough, especially since we were on a deadline. But the team kept pushing until they found a new printing process that could recreate the actual dips and valleys of Simone's sculpture in a layer of resin (and then sprinted on the rest to still hit the launch date!)
2. When the team decided how to crop & place the sculpture on the card, they put the most textured area where your thumb naturally lands. Nobody will ever consciously notice that, but I just love that someone thought about it.

That's what craft means at Mercury: not an aesthetic, not a value on a slide. It's striving for the highest level of quality, even in details that most people will never notice.

Wow Mercury commissioned a ceramicist to translate a handmade sculpture into 5,000 limited edition actual credit cards 👀

So they built a new printing process with Thales instead - taking the sculpture and the card gets a resin bed FIRST, then the artwork prints on top, so highlights sit on real raised texture.

posts.content:
Last week, I grabbed coffee with two co-founders who are about to head into their senior year at college, whilst also building a venture-backed startup. 

I marvel at this most complex of juggling acts but what they shared on why they are doing this and how, was eye-opening. 

There was a reassuring amount of cynicism towards traditional education (very relatable, as this is how I felt at university) and a recognition of the value in it (network effects, the people they’ve met, memories made). They also feel more empowered than ever as founders with the tools they have at their disposal, notably agents. 

Agents allow them to outsource the trivial and tedious busy work, meaning they can spend their time on the work that will really move the needle for their business. Agents also allow them to get things done whilst they are in class. I started to feel rather envious!

Mercury’s latest report, titled “The new economics of starting up 2026”, further validates this anecdotal evidence. 

Of the 1,500 U.S. founders and startup operators surveyed, 95% have deployed agents. Our report also highlighted that at the earlier stages, AI can have a significant impact and becomes a distinct economic advantage.

For a decade, Rafi T. thought of software the way most people think about plumbing: invisible, functional, not worth a thought. His experience with a new browser broke that first. 

Now, he uses AI to help create the same jolt for his customers on FUEGO.io — an AI-native platform that turns any brand's Shopify store into a fully custom mobile app in minutes, no trade-off between fast and generic, or custom and slow.

posts.content:
👀 This year’s New Economics of Starting Up is out: https://lnkd.in/g-ecPiny

I lead Stories at Mercury, and this report is becoming one of my favorite things we make. It’s a bit of a labor of love: a bunch of people who are deeply compelled to understand the evolving economics and mechanics of making startups work get completely engrossed in some data, go enthusiastically overboard in word count... 

And then pull it back enough to (hopefully!) help founders and entrepreneurs and others in the earlier years of building companies understand that landscape and where they fit in it.

This year, we surveyed 1,500 early-stage founders and startup builders. We sliced the data every which way, chased down things that made us go “huh” (tbh, lots of things make me go “huh”), and even pulled a few cuts of Mercury’s own data to go deeper.

A couple stand-outs:
 ✨  We weren’t looking for some grand AI story, but it’s wild to see the gap between the companies that are adopting AI and those that aren’t. Significant AI adopters were more confident in their businesses. They were more than 4x as likely to have raised venture capital. And founders whose companies were using AI were much more likely to pay themselves a market-rate salary. (Correlation ≠ causation, but fascinating nonetheless!)
 🫶  I also found it heartening to see that junior talent might be in a better spot than some headlines would have you think. At least if they’re looking for jobs at early-stage companies! 82% of companies said they’re hiring the *same number or more* early-career workers than they would have without AI. Maybe more interesting: significant AI adopters were twice as likely as moderate adopters to say they were hiring more junior people *because* of AI. Early-career folks, maybe the startup world is for you?

 🖼️ We also worked with artist and designer Enigmatriz to create a visual world that gets at a broader story of these economic and financial elements through things (well, birds) taking flight, collecting pieces, moving together and apart. The art is (in my totally unbiased opinion, of course) gorgeous. 

Anyway, there’s a lot in the report: business costs and expectations, why companies are holding onto more cash, changes in customer behavior, the fact that 95% (!!) of these early-stage companies have deployed AI agents, and more. Delighted to share it with you. I hope you learn something like I did.

Big ups to crew who worked on bringing it to life — including Megan Duffy, Kate Apostolou, Prateek Parashar, Amy Kirkham, Celeste Carswell (Thibault), Tamara Rahoumi, and many more.

Hannah had three budgets on one card and no idea which one dinner was about to hit.

She was at a Mercury onsite, testing the thing she'd spent months designing. Budgets is new in Mercury: rather than issuing an employee three cards for three purposes, a company sets money aside for each purpose — the lunch perk, the onsite, the office coffee run — and all of it lives on one card, each with its own limits and its own rules. Which is elegant right up until you're standing in a restaurant holding a bill that could plausibly belong to two of them, waiting to learn whether the system you built can tell the difference.

"The push notification came through and it had routed it to my lunch perk as expected, and also took care of categorization automatically, and automatically attached my receipt from my Gmail inbox because of our receipt matching feature," said Hannah Johnson, a product designer on Budgets. "I felt informed and relieved that everything had been automatically taken care of for me. Magical was definitely the feeling."

Most spend tools are built for the people in control — the finance leads, the admins, the controllers — while the employee experience gets sorted out afterward, which is how you end up with someone at a register trying to remember which card they're supposed to be using. Hannah's team started from the other end, on the premise that employees shouldn't have to think about the mechanics of company spending at all: they should know what they can spend on and how much, buy the thing, and trust that everything downstream gets handled.

So it gets handled. An auto-router reads the transaction and decides which budget it belongs to. Categorization happens on its own. Receipts match themselves out of your inbox, or arrive as a photo you text back. The only moment that asks anything of you is the one where your phone tells you it's already done.

“A principle across this work has been meeting employees where they are,” Hannah said. “These are people who are out running errands for the office, at onsites, at sales dinners, traveling. Given that, it felt important that our communication be really respectful and not overwhelming, but still reach them in the moments where it’s useful.”

posts.content:
Great design are two words thrown around a lot in startup land. Everyone is designing with care and intention but what that looks like in practice can vary.

Perhaps what great design looks like to me is different to you, perhaps that's what taste is? 

According to my Apple dictionary, taste is: the ability to discern what is of good quality or of a high aesthetic standard. But who then is the arbiter of taste?

I don't have the answer to that question but what I do know is that Mercury's special edition IO card epitomises incredibly thoughtful design.

A business is built on a strong foundation... what better material to embody that than stone?

“The early brainstorming was very open-ended and conceptual. We [even] considered whether we might be able to make the card partly out of stone”
- Serena E., Senior Brand Designer at Mercury

I think this perfectly encapsulates why I admire our creative people at Mercury so much. They aren't just thinking about how we could make something look like stone, they are exploring whether it's possible to create a card out of stone. 

Perhaps one day a card will be carved from stone, until that day our team ended up partnering with western Massachusetts-based ceramicist Simone Bodmer-Turner on a sculpture.

“The sculpture draws from the ceramic tools I use every day,” Simone says, “forms that are often kidney-shaped or defined by negative space and expand them into something much larger. That connected naturally with Mercury’s own thinking about money as a tool for building businesses.”

The story of how the sculpture's design found its way on to our special edition card deserves a far more eloquent and in depth deep dive, thankfully that exists.

Please go and give it a read. It's a testament to craft, the joy of making things, and great design that embodies so much more than just a card.

She’ll use AI to plan a road trip, trivia and all. To stop being “human middleware” between her firm’s previously disconnected systems. And she still doesn’t use it to handle her clients’ actual money.
______

Megan Murray spent 15 years in corporate finance before founding Leoluna Finance Collective, a fractional CFO practice built to fix a problem she kept seeing: founders piecing together a dozen disconnected vendors and still not getting real strategic support.

We talked to Megan as part of our Mercury Movement ambassador series. Read on for a few more takeaways that we just had to share:

Q: Fast-forward 2 years. What product will founders wonder how they ever lived without?
A: Something that continuously synthesizes information across the business — finance, sales, HR, Slack — and surfaces what needs attention before founders even know to ask. "The companies that win won't necessarily have more data. They'll have better systems for turning data into decisions."

Q: How are you actually using AI day-to-day — not the LinkedIn version?
A: To eliminate repetitive work, not replace expertise — data cleanup, formatting, documentation. Everything client-facing still gets human review.

Q: What's one AI workflow that feels like a cheat code right now?
A: Anything that turns "copy, paste, clean, format, repeat" into a one-click process. The real gain isn't fewer hours worked — it's fewer hours spent as human middleware between software systems, and more time on judgment and strategy.
